interactions.label: A patient develops sudden onset contralateral hemiplegia predominantly affecting

params.question: A patient develops sudden onset contralateral hemiplegia predominantly affecting the face and arm, accompanied by aphasia. Occlusion of which artery best explains this clinical picture?

answers.text: Anterior cerebral artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial cortex. Its territory strokes cause leg-dominant contralateral weakness, not the face-arm-aphasia pattern seen here.

answers.text: Middle cerebral artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The MCA covers the lateral cortex, including the motor strip for the face and arm and the language areas. Dominant hemisphere MCA occlusion adds aphasia to the contralateral motor deficit.

answers.text: Posterior cerebral artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital lobe. Its occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia, not hemiplegia with aphasia.

answers.text: Basilar artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Basilar artery occlusion produces brainstem signs — bilateral motor deficits, cranial nerve palsies, and impaired consciousness — not a unilateral hemispheric syndrome.

overallFeedback.feedback: Consider which artery covers the lateral cortex including the motor strip for the face and arm and the language areas. Dominant hemisphere involvement adds aphasia to the deficit.
The MCA supplies the lateral cortex and is the commonest site of ischaemic stroke. Dominant hemisphere occlusion explains face and arm weakness together with aphasia.

interactions.label: A patient is brought to casualty having woken with left-sided weakness at 7 am.

params.question: A patient is brought to casualty having woken with left-sided weakness at 7 am. Her family confirms she was completely normal when she went to sleep at 11 pm. Which time should be used to determine thrombolysis eligibility?

answers.text: 7 am — the time the deficit was discovered

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Discovery time is not the same as onset time. Using 7 am treats only an eight-hour delay as having elapsed, but the patient's last-known-well time was actually earlier.

answers.text: 3 am — the midpoint between sleeping and waking

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The midpoint is employed only in specific imaging-guided late-window protocols using DWI-FLAIR mismatch. Standard clinical practice uses the last-known-well time, not a calculated midpoint.

answers.text: 11 pm — when she was last confirmed neurologically normal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. For a wake-up stroke, the thrombolysis clock starts from the last-known-well time — the most recent moment the patient was confirmed normal. In this case that is 11 pm.

answers.text: Time of arrival at the emergency department

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Arrival time has no bearing on biological onset. Using it would allow any patient to appear eligible simply by arriving early, which is clinically meaningless.

overallFeedback.feedback: Ask when the patient was LAST KNOWN WELL — the most recent time a witness confirmed normal neurology. For a wake-up stroke that is when she fell asleep, not when she was discovered with the deficit.
The last-known-well time — 11 pm — starts the thrombolysis clock. For wake-up strokes, this is when the patient was last confirmed neurologically normal, not when the deficit was found.

interactions.label: A normal non-contrast CT scan of the brain reliably rules out ischaemic stroke.

params.question: A normal non-contrast CT scan of the brain reliably rules out ischaemic stroke.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: NCCT does not exclude ischaemia. Early ischaemic changes are commonly invisible on CT for many hours after onset. The scan's role in acute stroke is to rule out haemorrhage before thrombolysis — nothing more. Diffusion-weighted MRI detects ischaemia within minutes of onset.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. NCCT detects haemorrhage, not ischaemia. Early ischaemic strokes may be invisible on CT for 24–48 hours. A normal scan confirms only that it is safe to proceed with thrombolysis on imaging grounds.

interactions.label: A 65-year-old presents within 3 hours of stroke onset with an NIHSS score of 12.

params.question: A 65-year-old presents within 3 hours of stroke onset with an NIHSS score of 12. Her blood pressure is 188/108 mmHg and there are no other contraindications. What is the correct immediate management?

answers.text: Administer alteplase immediately — this blood pressure is within acceptable limits for thrombolysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The threshold for thrombolysis is a systolic below 185 mmHg. At 188 mmHg the systolic exceeds the limit; proceeding without treatment first increases the risk of haemorrhagic transformation.

answers.text: Withhold thrombolysis permanently — elevated blood pressure at this level is an absolute contraindication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is a relative barrier, not an absolute contraindication. Elevated blood pressure at this level can be corrected rapidly with IV labetalol, after which thrombolysis can proceed.

answers.text: Lower blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg before giving alteplase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The target before thrombolysis is below 185/110 mmHg, not 140/90. Aggressive lowering in acute stroke reduces perfusion to the ischaemic penumbra and may extend the infarct.

answers.text: Give intravenous labetalol to bring blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg, then administer alteplase

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A systolic of 188 mmHg exceeds the 185 mmHg threshold by a small margin. IV labetalol brings it into the safe range within minutes, allowing alteplase to be given without further delay.

overallFeedback.feedback: The blood pressure threshold for thrombolysis is below 185/110 mmHg. At 188/108 the systolic is marginally over the limit — treat with IV labetalol first, then give alteplase. Never confuse this with the 140/90 target used in other hypertensive settings.

The thrombolysis-specific threshold is below 185/110 mmHg — stricter than the permissive 220/120 used when withholding treatment. At 188/108, IV labetalol resolves the barrier quickly; this is not a reason to withhold treatment permanently.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden headache, ataxia, and vomiting. C

params.question: A 58-year-old hypertensive man develops sudden headache, ataxia, and vomiting. CT brain shows a 3.5 cm cerebellar haematoma. He is becoming progressively drowsy. What is the most appropriate management?

answers.text: Conservative management with blood pressure control and close neurological observation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Conservative management is appropriate for most supratentorial haemorrhage, but a cerebellar haematoma greater than 3 cm with neurological deterioration requires urgent surgery. The confined posterior fossa leaves no room for expansion.

answers.text: Urgent surgical decompression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cerebellar haemorrhage greater than 3 cm with neurological deterioration is a surgical emergency. The posterior fossa is a confined space; untreated haematoma expansion compresses the brainstem and is rapidly fatal.

answers.text: Intravenous alteplase to dissolve the haematoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Alteplase is absolutely contraindicated in haemorrhagic stroke. Administering it would expand the haematoma and would almost certainly be fatal.

answers.text: Nimodipine infusion to prevent vasospasm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nimodipine is used in subarachnoid haemorrhage to prevent delayed cerebral vasospasm. It has no role in intracerebral haemorrhage and would not address the space-occupying haematoma.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical distinction is posterior fossa versus supratentorial. The STICH trials found no benefit from early craniotomy in supratentorial haemorrhage; but the posterior fossa has no tolerance for haematoma expansion, making surgery urgent above 3 cm with deterioration.

Cerebellar haemorrhage greater than 3 cm with deterioration is a surgical emergency. The posterior fossa is a confined space — even moderate haematomas compress the brainstem. This surgical threshold is far lower than for supratentorial haemorrhage.

interactions.label: Three weeks after a left MCA stroke, a patient has Broca's aphasia and right hem

params.question: Three weeks after a left MCA stroke, a patient has Broca's aphasia and right hemiplegia. His wife asks whether he will recover his speech. Which response is most appropriate?

answers.text: "He will not regain speech — the left hemisphere damage is permanent."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This overstates certainty and is factually inaccurate. The brain retains neuroplasticity and the capacity to reorganise. Broca's aphasia with preserved comprehension does not carry a uniformly poor prognosis for expression.

answers.text: "It is impossible to say anything at this stage — we will have to wait and see."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vague non-answers fail the family entirely. A physician owes the caregiver a framework for planning even while honestly acknowledging the limits of prediction. This response leaves the family without the guidance they need.

answers.text: "Broca's aphasia with preserved comprehension carries a reasonable prognosis for regaining expression with intensive speech therapy."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Preserved comprehension is a favourable prognostic sign — the language comprehension network is intact. Intensive, task-specific speech therapy during the sub-acute neuroplasticity window exploits cortical reorganisation to restore expression.

answers.text: "Speech recovery requires transfer of function to the right hemisphere, which rarely succeeds after the age of 60."

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Right hemisphere recruitment is one mechanism of recovery but not the only one. Stating it rarely succeeds after 60 is an inaccurate generalisation that is not supported by the evidence taught in this module and is unnecessarily pessimistic.

overallFeedback.feedback: Avoid both poles: false certainty that rules out recovery, and vague deflection that offers no planning framework. Broca's aphasia with preserved comprehension has a more favourable prognosis than global aphasia — communicate that, while acknowledging genuine uncertainty.

Preserved comprehension in Broca's aphasia signals that Wernicke's area and the comprehension network are intact. Intensive speech therapy during the sub-acute neuroplasticity window gives a reasonable expectation of regaining expression — this is the framework the family needs.
